chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hajjal, from Tha'laba ibn Maymun, from Abd al-A'la ibn A'yan who said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'The one who does not recognize anything — is there anything upon him?' He said: 'No.'

key_terms.شَيْءٌ: Anything — used twice: first to denote ignorance of religious teachings, then to denote liability or obligation upon that person
key_terms.هَلْ عَلَيْهِ: Is there upon him — a jurisprudential formula asking whether a religious duty or accountability exists
key_terms.يَعْرِفْ: To recognize/know — here referring to recognition of religious obligations, the Imam, or fundamental truths of the faith

ai.seo_question: Is a person who is ignorant of religious duties held accountable in Islam?
ai.summary: In this hadith, Abd al-A'la ibn A'yan — brother of the famous jurist Zurarah and a companion of Imam al-Sadiq — poses a fundamental theological question about religious accountability: is a person who has no knowledge of religious obligations held responsible? The Imam's terse reply — 'No' — establishes the Shia jurisprudential principle that religious obligation is contingent upon knowledge. This question arose in the context of early Shia debates about the nature of divine proof (hujja) and when exactly religious duty becomes binding. For the original audience, this meant that someone who had genuinely never encountered Islam's teachings — or had no access to the Imam's guidance — bore no legal accountability before God.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, from Al Hajjal, from Sa’alba Bin Maymoun, from Abdul A’ala Bin Ayn who said,
